This Is the Family Tree of the World’s Fastest Runway-Launched Jet Aircraft
20 photos
Photo: Hermeus
For a number of years now, an American aviation company called Hermeus has been occasionally making the headlines thanks to its work on something that would ultimately become not only the fastest runway-launched jet aircraft in history, but also the world's fastest operational aircraft of any kind, period.
Over these rather short years, the company has managed to reach several milestones, but, in doing so, it also created a bit of confusion, at least for outside eyes, regarding its products and plans. Luckily, earlier this month, Hermeus detailed each of the prototypes it has made and will make before the actual production jet is ready.
A sort of family tree, if you will, of an aircraft design that could change military aviation, and, if the Gods allow, the civilian one as well.
Quarterhorse Mk 0 The first test prototype the company has ever made, the Quarterhorse Mk 0, ended its testing period in the final months of 2023. Although it was powered by a General Electric J-85 jet engine, it didn't actually fly, but did run up and down the runway several times over a period of 37 days.
The design was used by Hermeus engineers to determine what it would take, going forward, when it comes to manufacturing, integration, and test processes. It also provided the team working on the project with data on airframe design, engine control, and wireless communication.
Quarterhorse Mk 1 Photo: Hermeus Building on that, Hermeus created the next iteration of the Quarterhorse , the Mk 1. It, too, powered by a General Electric J-85 jet engine and imagined in a delta wing configuration, took to the sky over the Edwards Air Force Base in the spring of 2025.
The flight was not about performance and breaking records, but about informing Hermeus about things like ground and flight controls and their behavior during take-off, flight, and landing.
Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 The next iteration of the design, the Mk 2, switched engines, going for a Pratt & Whitney F100, and grew to be about the same size as an F-16, from which it borrowed some components, including the landing gear.
As the first of three planned aircraft from the Mk 2 iteration, this uncrewed plane managed to reach supersonic speeds in May 2026, more specifically Mach 1.21 (928 mph/1,494 kph). It then steadily increased speeds in subsequent flights, reaching Mach 1.6 (1,227 mph/1,975 kph). The design also flew with an undisclosed payload, previewing the way the production version will work.
Quarterhorse Mk 2.2 Photo: Hermeus Just two months ago from the time of writing, in September 2026, an improved Mk 2.2 Quarterhorse began testing using upgraded avionics, software, and the so-called Gryphon propulsion system.
Mentioned for the first time by Hermeus in an operational setting, the Gryphon is a precooler-turbine based on the Pratt & Whitney F100 engine. Comprising an actuated spike inlet and the engine itself, it allows proper operation at a range of speeds that are inaccessible to regular turbines.
Hermeus presently uses this design to validate the propulsion architecture that would eventually take the aircraft past the Mach 2 (1,534 mph/2,469 kph) barrier.
Quarterhorse Mk 2.3 This upcoming version of the design is being imagined as a means to test thermal management of the jet, and it will be built using new concepts and materials. The focus of the testing program for this one will also include the collection of data on stability and control as it will approach Mach 3 (2,301 mph/3,704 kph), meaning ramjet speeds.
Quarterhorse Mk 3 and Mk 4 Photo: Hermeus This is when the company's F100–based Chimera ramjet technology, which until now has only been tested on the ground, will come into play in the air. This powertrain will operate in turbine mode at low speeds and in ramjet mode as soon as higher-Mach speeds are reached.
Hermeus says the Mk 3 will be built around an all-new high-temperature airframe, and that it will use the Chimera II turbine-based combined-cycle (TBCC) propulsion system. This will make it, for all intents and purposes, the first aircraft to use such a design, and, if everything works according to plan, the fastest runway-launched jet in history.
The Mk 4, using the lessons learned with the Mk 3, will try to maintain ramjet speeds for longer at higher altitudes, setting the stage for the world's fastest operational aircraft, the ultimate goal of this project, to come into play. For now, this uncrewed drone, if you will, is referred to as the Darkhorse .
It's unclear when the production versions will be ready, but when it gets here, it will be capable of hitting Mach 5 (3,800 mph/6,100 kph). This will make it a very valuable tool for the needs of the American defense industry, but, sadly, it seems plans for a civilian version are no longer in play, at least not in the foreseeable future.
When it first made the headlines, Hermeus talked about something called the Halcyon, a commercial aircraft capable of carrying a small number of passengers at insane speeds, fast enough to cover the distance from London to New York, for instance, in just one and a half hours. As a reminder, it takes present-day aircraft some eight hours to do this today.
